Sandglass master list

Every element, what it is, and what it does with every other element. This page is built from the game's own data, so it always matches the game.

141 elements 3149 pairs that interact No problems in the last audit (59,643 test runs)
MatrixElementsWorld rulesAudit

Who reacts with whom

Each square is one pair. Its colour says what happens when they touch. Point at a square to read the details; click it to open the element.

Burns or explodesOne sets the other alight, or feeds its fire
Heat changeOne is hot or cold enough to melt, boil, freeze or ignite the other
Puts out fireWater smothers flames and flashes into steam
AcidAcid eats metal, rock or wood, or a gas turns water into acid
NeutralisesAcid and base cancel into water
Dissolves or thawsA solid goes into a liquid, or salt melts ice
Soaks upA porous powder takes in a liquid
Sets hardA powder takes in water and hardens, as cement does
Rusts or rotsA slow change where water or oxygen touches it
PoisonsA toxic gas kills living things
Special ruleA hand-written reaction
Sinks throughNo reaction; the heavier one ends up below
NothingThey only share heat by touch

    Sand

    powders powder

    Hardness

    Water

    liquids liquid

    A runny liquid. Flows and settles flat. Boils into steam when hot, freezes into ice when cold, and cools what it touches.

    State
    Liquid, 1,000 kg/m³
    In liquids
    Sinks through liquids lighter than 1,000 kg/m³, floats on heavier ones
    Falls
    up to 165 cells/s
    Boils
    at 100 °C, into steam
    Freezes
    below 0 °C, into ice
    Conducts
    only when it carries salt; current then splits it into hydrogen and oxygen
    Dissolves
    soluble powders (salt, sugar), up to each one’s limit; saltier is heavier

    Ice

    solids solid

    Frozen water, a cold solid. Stays put. Chills what it touches and melts back into water as it warms.

    State
    Solid, 917 kg/m³
    Starts at
    -20 °C
    Melts
    at 0 °C, into water

    With other elements (26)

    • Water Ice (-20 °C) is cold enough to freeze water into ice.
    • Steam Ice (-20 °C) is cold enough to condense steam into water. Steam (150 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.
    • Lava Ice (-20 °C) is cold enough to freeze lava into stone. Lava (1,200 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.
    • Fire Fire (850 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.
    • Smoke Smoke (150 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.
    • Salt Salt melts ice: dissolved, it lowers the freezing point.
    • Sugar Sugar melts ice: dissolved, it lowers the freezing point.
    • Spark Spark (300 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.
    • Molten copper Ice (-20 °C) is cold enough to freeze molten copper into wire. Molten copper (1,200 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.
    • Molten gold Ice (-20 °C) is cold enough to freeze molten gold into gold. Molten gold (1,150 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.
    • Molten aluminium Ice (-20 °C) is cold enough to freeze molten aluminium into aluminium. Molten aluminium (750 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.
    • Molten lead Ice (-20 °C) is cold enough to freeze molten lead into lead. Molten lead (400 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.
    • Molten wax Ice (-20 °C) is cold enough to freeze molten wax into wax. Molten wax (80 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.
    • Baking soda Baking soda melts ice: dissolved, it lowers the freezing point.
    • Caramel Caramel (190 °C) is hot enough to melt ice into water.

                  World rules

                  What holds everywhere, for every element.

                  • Room temperature is 20 °C. Empty cells are air. Air slowly drifts back to room temperature, which is how hot things cool and steam condenses.
                  • Air feeds fire with oxygen strength 0.20999999344348907. Burning turns touching air into smoke, which feeds nothing, so a sealed space runs out of air.
                  • Edges: the bottom and sides are walls. Smoke leaves through the top edge; other gases stay.
                  • Gravity is per element: each falling element has its own acceleration and top speed.
                  • Heat flows by touch. Each element has a conductivity and a heat capacity. Burning cells also push heat into their neighbours.
                  • Nothing appears from nothing. Movement only swaps cells. Only reactions, burning and phase changes turn one element into another.
                  • Phase changes reverse into their source: whatever an element melts or boils into sets back into that same element.

                  Audit

                  Every pair of elements is run together for 5 seconds at room temperature, hot (800 °C) and cold (−60 °C). Anything that appears must follow from the rules, no matter may appear from nothing, and pairs that do not react must keep their exact cell counts.

                  No problems across 59,643 test runs.
